name: Jos Plateau
summary: Volcanic highland in central Nigeria with a cooler climate and tin-mining history.
description: The Jos Plateau is a granite and volcanic upland rising sharply above the surrounding plains. Tin and columbite mining shaped 20th-century Jos. The height brings lower temperatures, Irish potatoes and vegetables, and tourism. Gully erosion is a modern hazard.
character: Inselbergs, temperate crops, mining scars, tourism.
economy: Tourism, remnant mining, highland farming, Jos urban services.

name: Mambilla Plateau
summary: Nigeria's highest inhabited plateau on the Cameroon border in Taraba.
description: Mambilla is a grassland plateau with tea estates and a proposed mega hydropower project. Chappal Waddi (Gangirwal) in the Gashaka-Gumti / border highlands is often cited as Nigeria's highest peak. Access is via steep escarpment roads.
elevationNote: Plateau ~1,500–1,800 m; peaks above 2,000 m (Chappal Waddi ~2,419 m)
character: Tea, cattle, montane grassland, cloud forest fragments.
economy: Tea, livestock, proposed hydropower, limited tourism.

name: Mandara Mountains
summary: Volcanic range along the Nigeria–Cameroon border in southern Borno / northern Adamawa fringe.
description: The Mandara are culturally associated with hill peoples (Mandara, Sukur UNESCO cultural landscape on the Cameroon side). On the Nigerian side they form a rugged border highland above the Chad plains.
character: Terraced hills, volcanic plugs, border cultures.

name: Niger Delta
summary: Africa's largest wetland delta where the Niger meets the Atlantic; Nigeria's petroleum heartland.
description: The delta covers ~70,000 km² of mangrove, freshwater swamp, and barrier islands. It holds the bulk of Nigeria's oil and gas, a dense creek network, and highly politicised environmental and federal-revenue issues. Nine states are commonly listed as 'Niger Delta' in policy, with a core of Bayelsa, Rivers, and Delta.
elevationNote: Mostly near sea level; tidal mangrove
character: Mangrove, oilfields, riverine settlements, barrier islands.
economy: Oil and gas, fisheries, boat transport, refining.

name: Sokoto Basin
summary: Semi-arid sedimentary basin of the northwest drained by the Sokoto–Rima system.
description: Cretaceous–Tertiary sediments underlie millet, sorghum, and irrigated fadama. The basin is drought-prone and depends on dams and groundwater. It is the core landscape of the Caliphate northwest.
character: Sahel–Sudan plains, seasonal rivers, irrigation schemes.
economy: Grain, livestock, onions (dry-season irrigation), limited oil exploration historically.

name: Guinea Savanna
summary: Wooded savanna belt between southern rainforest and northern Sudan/Sahel savanna.
description: Guinea savanna (southern and northern Guinea) is Nigeria's broad middle belt: shea, yam, sorghum, and cattle routes. Rainfall is typically 900–1,500 mm. It includes much of Kwara, Niger, Kogi, Benue, Nasarawa, and parts of Kaduna and FCT.
character: Parkland trees, seasonal burn, mixed farming.
economy: Yam, shea, grains, livestock corridors, Abuja hinterland.
